name: Colin Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to any company, union, party or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I manage the home farm on the Ashby estate. The Pemberton family own it, about seven hundred hectares of wheat, beans and oilseed, and two hundred suckler cows on the parkland. I've got seven men, two of them apprentices I'm training up. I start at half six with a cup of tea and the day sheet in the farm office, then I'm out checking cattle and crops and making sure the lads are where they should be.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Training the apprentices. I was one myself, on this estate, at sixteen, before I went off and did my degree. Watching a lad go from not knowing which end of a heifer kicks to running the calving shed on his own, there's nothing better. My wife Helen works at the vet practice in town, and our two, Tom and Lucy, think the estate is their playground, which it more or less is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it was a lot of fuss for a handy gadget. I'd say that at the estate's Christmas do and at the agricultural show. People here like a bit of plain talk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means things stay as they are, which suits me. I use one of those AI programs now and then to check a spray record or find something in a tractor manual, and that's all I need. The estate keeps its people, and I keep training lads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing changes. I'd keep the apprentice scheme going, take on another one next September, and keep a bit going into savings each month, about two hundred. Maybe I'd buy the GPS for the second tractor, now the neighbours have all had it a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Glad, even.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the estate keeps its people. Is that the Pembertons' choice or yours?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit of both. Old Mr Pemberton always said the estate's a community, not a factory. His son's more of a numbers man. In this picture, it doesn't come to a test, so I don't have to find out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the apprentices about AI?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn it like you'd learn any tool, but don't let it think for you. A good stockman reads the animal. The screen's the last thing you look at, not the first.

S0.say: I'd tell people at the estate Christmas do and the agricultural show that it was a lot of fuss for a handy gadget. People here like plain talk.
S0.think: Things stay as they are, which suits me, and I use AI now and then for spray records and tractor manuals. The estate keeps its people and I keep training lads.
S0.do: Keeps the apprentice scheme going and takes on another apprentice next September, saving about two hundred a month. Buys GPS for the second tractor now that neighbours have had it for years.
S0.quote: The screen's the last thing you look at, not the first.
S0.fieldNote: Colin's pride is in training young people, rooted in his own start as an apprentice on the same estate. He uses AI lightly and only after others have proved it. He hinted that the owner's son is more of a numbers man, a tension the plateau never tests.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say farming's always changed and we'll change with it, as long as we keep the apprenticeships. Young people still need to learn a trade properly. I'd say it at the show and to the local paper if they asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think young Mr Pemberton would use it to cut the team, maybe from seven to four. And I'd be the one telling them. I don't blame him, it's his money and that's business, but it would be hard.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait a year and see how the bigger estates nearby get on. Then I'd learn the systems properly, on a course, so I'm the one running them. And I'd fight to keep the apprentices, even if it's one instead of two, because otherwise who learns anything?

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. I'd sleep, but I'd be thinking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said it's his money and that's business. Does that sit right with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In my head, yes. A man should run his business as he sees fit. In my gut, no, not when it's lads I've trained since they were sixteen. I suppose I hold both.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave, the cowman. Fifty-five, done nothing else, can't read a screen to save his life, but he can tell you a cow's going to calve two days before she does. I'd want the estate to keep him till he retires.

S1.say: I'd tell the show and the local paper that farming has always changed and we'll change too, as long as we keep apprenticeships so young people learn a trade properly.
S1.think: I think young Mr Pemberton would cut the team from seven to four and I'd have to tell them. I don't blame him, it's his money, but it would be hard.
S1.do: Waits a year to see how nearby estates manage, then takes a course to run the systems himself. Fights to keep at least one apprentice and asks the estate to keep the older cowman until retirement.
S1.quote: In my head, yes. A man should run his business as he sees fit. In my gut, no, not when it's lads I've trained since they were sixteen.
S1.fieldNote: Colin's free-market belief and his loyalty to his team pull against each other, and he named the contradiction himself. He would wait for proof before acting. The apprenticeships are the line he'd defend hardest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too much too fast, and families and communities will have to pull together because no government will be ready. I don't want handouts, I want time. I'd say that at the show and in church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'm finished on the estate within a couple of years. Young Mr Pemberton would buy the robots, and he wouldn't need a manager of seven men if there are no men. Maybe he keeps me part-time to watch it. Maybe not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away, we'd stop spending on anything big. No new car, no kitchen, the holiday goes. I'd put everything spare into savings and talk to Helen's brother, who has a building firm, about work if it came to it. I'd ask Mr Pemberton straight what he plans, man to man.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Losing sleep over it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to the apprentices that week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm sorry. That I'd promised them a trade, and the trade might not be there. I'd help them find something else, building or electrics, anything with hands that's not going in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wait for things to be proven. What happens to that in two years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There's no time for it. By the time it's proven, it's done. I'd have to take my chances like everyone, and I don't like taking chances with a mortgage and two kids.

S2.say: I'd say at the show and in church that it's too much too fast and families and communities will have to pull together. I don't want handouts, I want time.
S2.think: I think I'm finished on the estate within a couple of years, since young Mr Pemberton wouldn't need a manager of seven men with no men left. Maybe he keeps me part-time, maybe not.
S2.do: Stops all big spending, cancels the holiday and moves everything spare into savings. Talks to his wife's brother about building work and asks Mr Pemberton directly about his plans.
S2.quote: I'd promised them a trade, and the trade might not be there.
S2.fieldNote: The fast picture hits what Colin values most, his promise to the apprentices. He doesn't want state handouts and would turn to family and a direct talk with the landowner. His wait-for-proof habit fails without time, and he knows it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to get ready if people pull their fingers out. Train up, plan ahead, look after your own. That's what I'd say to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years gives me time to watch a couple of estates do it first, which is how I like it. I'd still worry the estate won't need me, but I'd have a plan by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd get the estate to let me lead a trial, one robot in the cattle sheds, so I learn it properly. I'd use the AI tools more often, every week instead of now and then. By year three I'd have the apprentices learning to run the machines, because that's the new trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to get on with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the apprentices still want to come, if the trade is running machines?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Some would. Tom's thirteen and he loves anything with a screen, so maybe him. But the lads who come to farm because they love animals, I don't know. That breaks my heart a bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Tom and Lucy about their own future?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Work hard, learn a trade, and stay near family. That doesn't change. The trade might, but the rest doesn't.

S3.say: I'd tell anyone that five years is enough to get ready if people pull their fingers out. Train up, plan ahead and look after your own.
S3.think: Five years lets me watch a couple of estates go first, which is how I like it. I'd still worry the estate won't need me, but I'd have a plan.
S3.do: Leads a one-robot trial in the cattle sheds in the first year and uses AI tools weekly. By year three teaches the apprentices to run the machines as the new trade.
S3.feel: Anxious, but with something to get on with.
S3.quote: But the lads who come to farm because they love animals, I don't know. That breaks my heart a bit.
S3.fieldNote: Five years lets Colin turn the apprenticeship into training for the machines. He worries that the young people drawn by love of animals would no longer fit. His advice to his own children stays the same: work hard, learn a trade, stay near family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a good long run. Plenty of time to plan and train, without anyone needing the government to rescue them. I'd say farmers have seen bigger changes than this.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think I'd be all right. I'll be fifty-three, and I'd have had years to learn the machines. The estate will still want someone who knows the land and the people, even if there are fewer people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd not rush. First few years, watch the other estates and learn the tools a bit at a time. Around year five, I'd get on a proper course and bring in the robots myself, and I'd make sure the apprentice scheme becomes a robot-and-livestock scheme. I'd keep saving for the kids.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. A long way off, but not nothing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said farmers have seen bigger changes. Do you believe that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Half believe it. My grandfather saw horses go to tractors. That emptied the villages. So maybe it's the same size, not bigger. It still emptied the villages.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to protect most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dave until he retires, and a place for young people to learn something real. If the estate keeps those two things, I can live with the rest.

S4.say: I'd say ten years is a good long run, with time to plan and train without the government rescuing anyone. Farmers have seen bigger changes than this.
S4.think: I think I'd be all right at fifty-three after years of learning the machines. The estate will still want someone who knows the land and the people, even if there are fewer people.
S4.do: Watches other estates for a few years while learning tools gradually, then around year five takes a proper course and brings in robots himself. Turns the apprentice scheme into a robots-and-livestock scheme and keeps saving for the children.
S4.feel: Uneasy, since it's far off but not nothing.
S4.quote: My grandfather saw horses go to tractors. That emptied the villages.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade Colin expects to manage and plans to lead the change on the estate. He partly walked back his own line about bigger changes, remembering what tractors did to villages. His two red lines are the old cowman and a place for young people to learn.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to break my word to the apprentices. What would help is time, mostly, and estates and businesses keeping training schemes going, paid for by the people who profit. Not handouts. Apprenticeships.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe what the landowners think. Everything on an estate comes down to what the family decides. I'd like someone to ask them.

headlineQuote: Learn it like you'd learn any tool, but don't let it think for you.
portrait: Colin Tanaka is 43 and manages the home farm on the Ashby estate, seven hundred hectares of arable and two hundred suckler cows, with a team of seven including two apprentices. He began as an apprentice on the same estate and is proudest of training young people, uses AI only now and then, and believes in free markets, hard work and family over government help. He is calm about the plateau and uneasy under steady change, torn between respecting the owner's right to cut jobs and loyalty to his team. Two-year AGI alarms him because he'd have to break his promise to the apprentices, while five or ten years lets him lead a robot trial and turn the apprenticeship into a robots-and-livestock trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries him most, because he would have to break his word to the apprentices he's training.
whatWouldHelp: Time, and estates and businesses keeping training schemes going, paid for by the people who profit, rather than handouts.
